arguments.message:
Matrix products need not commute, so $QP = I$ alone does not promise $PQ = I$. For square $P$ and $Q$ it does, because $Pv = 0$ forces $v = QPv = 0$, so $P^{-1}$ exists and

$$Q = Q(PP^{-1}) = (QP)P^{-1} = P^{-1}.$$

arguments.question:
With
$$R = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \quad\text{and}\quad S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},$$
the product $RS$ is the $2 \times 2$ identity. Is $SR$ the $3 \times 3$ identity, and why?
arguments.correctAnswer: No. $SR$ has rows $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,0)$, $(0,0,0)$: it sends $e_3$ to $0$. Reason: $SR$ first applies $R$, which maps $\mathbb{R}^3$ into $\mathbb{R}^2$ and kills $e_3$, so the map of $SR$ has a nonzero kernel and rank at most $2$, never $3$. The square-matrix argument fails because $R$ and $S$ are not square: $RS = I$ makes $S$ one-to-one, but a one-to-one $3 \times 2$ matrix has rank $2$, not $3$, so it cannot be onto $\mathbb{R}^3$ and has no two-sided inverse.

arguments.question: Three $3 \times 3$ matrices satisfy $UVW = I$. Is $U$ invertible, and why?
arguments.correctAnswer: Yes. Grouping the product as $U(VW) = I$ shows that the square matrix $VW$ is a one-sided inverse of the square matrix $U$. For square matrices a one-sided inverse is two-sided (from $U(VW) = I$, $VW$ is one-to-one, so it is invertible and its inverse is $U$), so $U$ is invertible with $U^{-1} = VW$, and also $VWU = I$.
